claim: At N=256, the accel_step margin over control first reached >= 0.1 at step 100 in both seeds (0.116 for seed 30, 0.104 for seed 29; both were 0.045-0.049 at step 50). That is the same step as the N=64 crossing, not later. Distance and energy formed by step 25. At step 600, accel_step R2 was 0.88-0.89 vs control 0.67-0.70 (margin 0.19-0.21, layer 3). Force never beat its control: R2 0.54-0.55 vs 0.51-0.54, margin 0.012-0.032, after a brief peak of 0.09 at step 50. Neither model beat the constant-velocity baseline (val_mse_ratio 3.12-3.20).
confidence_note: Both seeds ran all 600 planned steps and show the outcome expected if the hypothesis were false: accel_step crosses 0.1 at step <= 100. With N=16 crossing at steps 75-100 (f-20261011-231141-ab3a) and N=64 at step 100, formation timing looks roughly fixed across steps_per_orbit. Four things limit this. (1) Seed 29's crossing margin of 0.104 is barely over the threshold, and the probe trajectory only has points at steps 50 and 100. So a 'later' crossing that falls inside that window cannot be ruled out. Probes every 10 steps over the first 200 would settle it. (2) The hypothesis assumed the model would learn the N=256 task. It did not: val_mse_ratio is 3.1-3.2, which the hypothesis did not anticipate. That makes it hard to read timing as 'set by task demand'. (3) accel_step's random-control R2 is high (0.67-0.70). The margin may partly reflect orbit-scale information (a^3) present in the inputs rather than learned per-snapshot gravity. (4) The cross-N comparison uses different seeds. I would revise toward 'supported' if finer checkpoints showed N=256 crossing consistently after N=64 by more than the seed-to-seed spread, or if a better-normalized N=256 model that beats the baseline formed accel_step later.
